outputs.L1:
**From the Mithridatic Wars, First Century BC**

Our general was elsewhere, but we drowned.
While he rested, he shipped us home
with the bulk of his spoils
that had weighed his army down.
The thrashing storm
that caught us cracked the hulls
and made us offerings to the sea floor—
a rain of statues, gold, and men.

Released from service,
done with war,
the crash and hiss now muted,
we fell through streams of creatures
whose lives were their sole purpose.
We settled amid treasure looted
from the temples of rubbled Athenian Greece;
among us, bronze and marble gods and goddesses
moored without grace,
dodged by incurious fish.

Their power was never meant to buoy us—
our pleasures were but incidental gifts—
yet, shaken by their radiance in our dust,
we had surrendered them our voices.
Their faces, wings, and limbs
lie here beside our sanded bones
and motionless devices.

Little crabs endeavor to don rings
set with agate and amethyst,
and many an octopus,
seeking an hour of rest,
finds shelter in our brain-cases.
And so we are of use still.
outputs.L2:
**From the Mithridatic Wars, first century BC**

Our commander was somewhere far away, yet we perished beneath the waves.
During his period of rest, he sent us back toward home,
loaded down with the greater share of his plunder
that had slowed his marching troops.
The violent tempest
that overtook us split the ships apart
and turned us into gifts for the ocean's depths —
a shower of sculptures, precious metal, and human bodies.

Discharged now from duty,
finished with warfare,
the roar and foam grown quiet,
we sank past currents of living things
whose sole aim was simply to exist.
We came to rest alongside riches stolen
from the shrines of shattered Athenian Greece;
in our company, deities of bronze and stone,
male and female, anchored themselves without elegance,
avoided by indifferent fish.
Their divine force was never intended to keep us afloat —
whatever joy we felt was merely an accidental blessing —
but, stirred by their brilliance while we ground them into powder,
we had surrendered our voices to them.
Their countenances, their wings, their arms
rest in this place beside our sand-worn bones
and our lifeless machinery.

Tiny crabs try to slip on rings
mounted with agate and amethyst,
and countless octopuses,
hunting for a brief moment's peace,
take refuge within our skulls.
And so we serve a purpose even now.
outputs.L3:
# The Drowned Soldiers' Lament

We were coming home. That is the first thing you must understand—we had survived the Mithridatic Wars, endured the long campaigns in the East, and we were sailing back toward our own shores when the sea took us. A violent storm rose without mercy, and the waves hammered our ship until the hull cracked open beneath us. The water rushed in, cold and total, and we drowned together—soldiers who had outlived the sword only to be claimed by the storm.

Our general did not share our fate. He lived because he was not among us; he had gone by another route, sending his men ahead with the heavy burden of our victories. The spoils of war had weighed upon the army for too long—crate upon crate of plundered wealth—and so he dispatched us homeward with the treasure while he himself remained elsewhere. In this way, chance spared him and condemned us.

The ship carried the looted riches of conquered lands, the sacred plunder stripped from Greek temples we had emptied in our campaigns. Among the cargo were the images of the gods themselves: statues of bronze and marble, figures of gods and goddesses wrought by devoted hands and meant to stand in holy places. Now they lie scattered across the sea floor beside us, these divine forms sunk into the silence of the deep, far from any altar.

We do not curse them for our deaths. We understand now that these statues were never made to save us—they were never our protectors, only the plunder we carried. And yet there is a strange grief in it, for in our living days we had given our voices to the gods, had sung and prayed and worshipped the radiance these very figures were carved to honor. We devoted ourselves to their brightness, and in the end that brightness could not keep the water from our lungs.

Still, we are not entirely without purpose, even here. The sea has found its own use for what remains of us. Crabs creep among the sunken treasure and slip the jeweled rings upon their claws, trying on the wealth that once was ours. Octopuses drift into the hollows of our skulls and make their shelter there, curling into the empty spaces where our thoughts once lived. So we serve still, offering our bones and our riches to the creatures of the deep. Even in death, it seems, we are of some small use to the living world.
outputs.L4:
**The Cargo of the Drowned**

We do not speak, and yet we speak to you,
the ones who sank beneath the wine-dark swell
in that far year when Rome and Pontus warred,
when Mithridates raised his eastern crown
and Sulla's legions bled across the East.
A general—his name has left our lips,
worn smooth by salt and centuries of tide—
grew heavy with the plunder of the Greeks:
the marble limbs of gods torn from their shrines,
the bronze Apollos green with sacred age,
the temple silver, and the household lamps
that once lit rooms in cities now made ash.

He loaded us like ballast for the voyage home,
we soldiers, weary, dreaming of our farms,
of wives whose faces we had half-forgotten,
of olive groves and the slow Italian sun.
The holds were crammed with what was not our own—
looted divinities in wooden crates,
the wrenched-off faces of a conquered peace.

The storm came sudden as a god's contempt.
The mast split like a struck man's collarbone,
the black sea reared and took us in one throat.
We drowned among the very gods we stole,
our hands still reaching for the surface light
that dimmed and greened and finally went dark.

Now do not pity us. We rest at last.
No march, no muster, no centurion's shout,
no distant horn to wake us into blood.
We lie in sand as soft as any bed,
beside the marble Zeus, the bronze-cast Muse,
their calm eyes staring where no light arrives.
The plunder and the plunderers are one—
the same slow silt has settled on us both,
the same cold current combs our common hair.

And we have found a use we did not seek.
Through the round windows of our hollow skulls
the octopus draws in its folded arms
and makes a chamber of the house of thought.
Small crabs have taken lodging in our ribs
and scuttle where our beating hearts once were.
The little fish drift through us like a breath.

This is our peace: to shelter what still lives,
to give our emptiness away as home.
The gods we carried keep us company,
the sea has made us equal in the dark,
and loss, which seemed the end of everything,
became a quiet, endless usefulness—
a giving, when there was nothing left to give.
outputs.L5:
# From the Mithridatic Wars

The Mithridatic Wars were a series of three conflicts fought between the Roman Republic and the Kingdom of Pontus, ruled by King Mithridates VI Eupator, between 88 and 63 BCE. These wars represent one of the most significant challenges to Roman expansion in the eastern Mediterranean during the late Republic.

## The Rise of Mithridates VI

Mithridates VI of Pontus was a formidable adversary who controlled a substantial kingdom along the southern shore of the Black Sea. Ambitious and cunning, he sought to expand his influence throughout Asia Minor and challenge Roman authority in the region. He is remembered for his intelligence, his linguistic abilities, and his legendary immunity to poison, which he reportedly cultivated by consuming small amounts throughout his life.

## The Three Wars

**The First Mithridatic War (88–84 BCE)** began when Mithridates orchestrated the massacre of tens of thousands of Roman and Italian settlers in Asia Minor, an event known as the Asiatic Vespers. The Roman general Lucius Cornelius Sulla was dispatched to confront him, eventually forcing Mithridates to accept peace terms.

**The Second Mithridatic War (83–81 BCE)** was a shorter, less decisive conflict that arose from tensions and unfinished business between the two powers, primarily involving the Roman commander Lucius Licinius Murena.

**The Third Mithridatic War (73–63 BCE)** proved decisive. Roman generals Lucullus and later Pompey the Great campaigned against Mithridates, ultimately breaking his power. Facing defeat and betrayal, Mithridates died in 63 BCE.

## Legacy

The Mithridatic Wars significantly expanded Roman control in the East and demonstrated the growing military and political ambitions of individual Roman commanders. These conflicts contributed to the transformations that would eventually reshape the Republic itself.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem from the perspective of drowned soldiers whose shipwreck sank Greek treasures and statues to the sea floor during the Mithridatic Wars.
counterfactuals.output:
**Cargo of the Drowned**

We were the hands that bound the bronze in ropes,
that heaved the marble maidens down the plank,
war-loot bound for Rome—our captains' hopes—
before the black wave took us as we sank.

Now we keep court among the loot we stole.
The gods we carried lie beside us here,
their faces green with verdigris and cold,
their painted eyes gone hollow, year on year.

A horseman rears in silt without his horse.
A goddess trails a garden of pale weed.
The scales that dressed the fish are our remorse;
the current is the only prayer we read.

We do not sleep. We drift and count the drowned—
Pontic and Roman, equal in the brine,
who marched for Sulla, or for Mithridates crowned,
now share one grave, one salt, one broken line.

Above us, empires quarrel for a coast.
Below, the amphorae spill their ancient wine
to feed no lips. We are the mildest ghosts,
robbers robbed, whose plunder is not mine

nor any man's. The philosopher of bronze
still lifts one arm to lecture to the dark,
and no one listens but the passing swans
of silver mackerel, quick as any spark.

Remember us—or don't. The sea forgets.
It sanded down our names to blank and smooth.
We guard a beauty no one now regrets,
the loveliest lie, the deep and drowning truth:

that all the marble worlds men die to own
sink, in the end, past every claiming hand,
and lie with us, indifferent as stone,
in kingdoms that no soldier could command.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free-verse poem narrated by the dead sailors of an ancient shipwreck, reflecting on the looted temple gods that sank with them and the sea creatures that now inhabit their bones.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Water Keeps

We were forty men and one cargo of thieves' luck—
the gods we pried from marble sockets,
their gold eyes still watching
as the hull opened like a mouth.

Now we speak in the language of settling.
Our jaws unhinge with the current.
We have learned to say nothing
in a thousand small clicks of shifting bone.

The gods went down first, being heavier,
being made to sink into worship
or oblivion, whichever hands them lower.
Bronze Poseidon lies face-up in the silt,
still trident-armed, still furious,
learning what we learned too late—
that the sea does not accept authority,
only weight.

*

Something lives in the cage of my chest now.
An octopus has made a den of my ribs,
each night pulling shells across the opening
like a door drawn shut against the dark.
I do not mind. She is warmer than prayer.
She keeps house where my heart kept fear.

A moray threads the eye of our captain,
in and out of the socket that once
squinted at horizons, counted profit,
misjudged the anger of a stolen shrine.
The eel asks nothing. This is mercy.
The eel does not believe we deserved the storm.

*

We wonder sometimes—
in the long arithmetic of tide—
whether the gods feel it too:
the anemones softening their stern faces,
the coral thickening a raised stone hand
into something almost tender,
almost forgiving.

Maybe this is what worship becomes
when the worshippers are gone:
not incense, not blood,
but the patient masonry of polyps,
the slow gilding of rust,
a barnacle's small mouth
opening and closing
over the word for *holy*.

*

Do not raise us.
We have grown into the reef.
Our finger bones are branched with life,
our skulls are lanterns for the blind fish,
and the gods we wronged
lie beside us now, disarmed,
green-skinned, patient,
teaching us the only truth
the deep has ever offered:

that everything taken
is only borrowed light,
and the sea will have it back—
the plunder and the plunderer,
the idol and the eye,
all of it dissolved to the same slow silt,
all of it, at last,
belonging.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting first-century BC poem about a Roman ship carrying spoils of war that wrecked in a storm, told collectively by the drowned crew.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Cargo We Became

We do not speak as men speak now,
with breath. We speak as water speaks—
in the long syllable of the tide,
in the salt that finds your lips.

We carried gold from broken cities.
We carried gods torn from their altars,
their bronze eyes green with distances,
their mouths still open in a foreign prayer.

The general rode the deck like Caesar,
counting triumphs he would never march.
We rowed. We did not count. We were the counting—
the sum beneath his sum, the load below the load.

Then the sky unclasped its iron.
The sea stood up on its hind legs.
We saw the mast bow like a captured king
and heard the timbers speak the truth of trees:

*we too were forests once, we too were felled.*

The gods went first, indifferent, sinking
back toward the dark from which men dug them.
The gold went next, a slow bright rain,
each coin a little sun put out.

And we came after—Lucius, Gaius,
the boy whose name we cannot hold,
the Greek who cursed in his own tongue,
the man who prayed to no one and was answered.

Now we are ballast. Now we are the reef
where fish rehearse their silver drills.
Now we hold the spoils forever,
guardians who own nothing, not even our names.

Remember us, who are not remembered.
No column stands. No stone is cut.
Only the water keeps our shape,
pouring us endlessly toward a shore

we will not reach, have never reached,
are always in the act of reaching—
the drowned crew of a nameless ship,
speaking to you in the voice of rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem about a sunken cargo of stolen bronze and marble statues from plundered Athens, imagining the perspective of the soldiers who went down with them.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cargo of the Gods

We loaded them at dusk, the marble kings,
the bronze-limbed heroes wrenched from temple stone,
their marble eyes still bright with sunlit things—
Athens behind us, weeping, overthrown.

Our captain laughed and called them Caesar's due,
the spoils of empire, treasure for the crown.
We stacked the gods like grain, we bound them true,
and never thought that gods could drag us down.

The wind came black off Cape Malea's teeth.
The sea stood up. We heard the timbers groan.
And Nike spread her wings somewhere beneath
the swallowing dark, and would not fly alone.

I clung to Zeus, his cold and perfect arm,
as if a stolen god could still forgive—
as if the marble held some borrowed charm
to tell the drowning things how men should live.

Now Piraeus dreams above us, far and warm,
and here we lie where light forgets to reach:
a soldier's bones inside a hero's form,
our ransomed empire scattered on the beach

of some blind valley in the ocean's floor.
The statues do not mourn. They never will.
They kept their faces through the closing door.
We plundered them. They have us, softly, still.

The fish move through the general's parted lips.
Salt writes its slow inscription on the bronze.
And no one comes. The centuries, like ships,
pass overhead—the darkness, and the dawns—

while we hold vigil, thief beside his prize,
two kinds of stillness settling into one:
the carved, indifferent gaze that never dies,
the human eyes that never see the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary poem titled with a historical note, spoken by drowned men on the seabed, meditating on treasure, gods, mortality, and how crabs and octopuses now use their remains.
counterfactuals.output:
**On the wreck of the *San Bartolomé*, foundered off Cádiz, 1591, all hands lost with a cargo of Peruvian silver**

We are the chorus the water keeps,
tongueless, and yet we speak.
Lay your ear against the cold
and hear us gossip in the deep.

Once we were sailors, greedy men,
who counted coin against the dark.
The silver we would die to hold
is holding us. Regard our work:

each ingot furred a soft green now,
each doubloon a slow blind coin
the current tongues and will not spend.
We hoarded. Now we join

the ledger of the ledgerless.
Above us, weather. Below, the sand
that does not care what kings we crossed,
what gods we begged, what land.

We prayed to a bright particular Christ,
we prayed to Fortune, wind, and star,
and every prayer came back to us
as salt, as pressure, as we are.

A crab has made my skull his house.
He carries me and does not thank.
He wears my thought as furniture,
my eye a cellar, cool and blank.

An octopus, the ocean's monk,
has folded soft into my chest
where once a frightened engine ran—
he keeps his midden there, and rests.

He stacks my ribs with broken shell,
with one gold button, one white stone,
and tends this treasury of dross
more tenderly than we our own.

So this is where the wanting goes.
Not up, to any promised sphere,
but down, and sideways, into mouths,
into the patient, chewing year.

The gods we made to guard the gold
have silted over, mild and gone.
The sea has swallowed even them.
Only the salt keeps carrying on.

Listen: you who count your days
as coins, and think the count is you—
we are the sum of all that math.
We are the total. It came due.

Come down. The water will explain.
It has a way of making plain
how little of a man is man,
and how the rest is given, again,

to crab, to current, and to crab,
to the soft dark householders who thrive,
who take our absence for a gift,
who make our nothing come alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
